en: Now, for the purpose of establishing the deities such as Pratirūpa and others,
the construction of a large-walled hall with a small interior chamber is desired.
Now, for the purpose of enshrining deities such as statues and the like, one desires to construct small or large buildings with walled enclosures.
According to the measurement of the length of the shanks, there are proclaimed divisions starting from four sections up to thirty-six sections, categorized as the smallest and so forth.
According to the dimensions of the supporting ground, one should construct [the mandala] from four *dhanus* up to thirty-six *dhanus*, distinguishing between the small and other sizes.
A wooden rod made of one cubit, together with the first three finger-breadths of the person of supreme proportions, is called a *kāṇḍākāṣṭhā*.

When the fingers and so forth of a person of standard proportions are joined together to form one cubit, it is called a "cubit-measure" (*śamyā*) and may also be referred to as an "arrow-shaft" (*iṣu*).
Then, the smallest [stūpas] are proclaimed to be twelve cubits in extent;
thereafter, the middling ones are twenty-four cubits in extent.
That which culminates in twelve cubits is known as the small [size]; that which culminates in twenty-four cubits is the medium [size].
Those extending up to thirty-six cubits are, therefore, proclaimed as the best.

The distinction among these is as follows: the shanks are increased by beautiful increments, reaching a maximum of thirty-six cubits; this is renowned as the most excellent. Through these divisions, the portion of the ground for the pedestal is increased here.
The legs should be made as a single mass, consisting of sixteen wooden blocks.
Outside the four-square inner chamber,
the walls are formed by the surrounding squares.
Generally, the increases for the walls are considered to be by one-quarter of the part;
however, they should be made even greater where the upper load is heavy.
With many parts of his feet, he desires to increase the walls; wherever there is a great burden above, there too an excess must be performed.
Even without a girdle, these shanks are not beautiful without wandering; but when that [wandering] is present, they are like a waist-belt for the Nandana grove, possessing five parts.
It is not beautiful without a supporting courtyard or a chamber; where these exist, one should place the fivefold girdle of joy around the waist.
The gods appear there without crowding, together with their splendors; and for the sake of that universal renown, the gateway is made long.
Because the gods perceive it simultaneously with its light without contradiction, and for the sake of making it renowned to all, the entrance to that meaning is indeed remote.
When the deity has arisen, that which is considered unobstructed is the half-doorway; for one who is seated, it should not exceed the measure of a living being.

Wherever it is not in conflict with the deities, its very erection is rightly desired; the measurement of the wood for the half-door should be such that it does not exceed the vicinity [of the threshold].
The length of the door is commended when it does not obstruct the deity;
it is also commended when it does not obstruct worshippers who are very few in number.
Because there is no contradiction with the deity, the remote method has been explained; since even those that are extremely small are not contradictory, the objects of worship have also been taught.

The height of the shank is measured as being equal to its width;
however, in some cases, a reduction in width should be made according to aesthetic requirements.
The height of the support is equal to the width of the support; having correctly gathered the expansive dance, it should be made beautiful and harmonious in its beauty.
The rotation of the doors and other elements has been described by the ancient teachers as being performed by the fourth,
sixth, and eighth parts in the cases known as *kanīyasī* and the others.
The masters of old have taught the application [of prefixes] such as *pra* to words like *dvāra*; through their four, six, and eight parts, they are known as "small" (*hīna*) and so forth.
Because the wall was too narrow, that [measurement] was stated differently; indeed, they do not become beautiful through walls that are either too narrow or too wide.
It is taught that the walls should be either very small or very extensive, and not otherwise; for those that are extremely small or excessively large will not be beautiful.
In every case, the door is prescribed to be one-fourth part;
likewise, in the Kīrti [temple] with its eight sections (aṣṭakāṇḍā), the door is observed in that very same way.

It is not asserted that there are openings on all sides by virtue of being a mere portion of the fourth part; rather, as is well known, it is asserted to have eight petals and likewise [openings] at those very locations.
In the three types of temples known as *trikīrti*, the door should be made with a portion equal to one part out of the two parts specified;
for those starting from ten cubits, the door should be made somewhat larger or even larger than that.

Regarding the single set of garments prescribed for those two cubits, it is known as the "three equal parts. Here, one should make the openings for ten [fingers] and so forth; that which is slightly larger than this is the "excessive" [measure].
Then, the doors and other features should be joined with the middle [section] by means of exactly one-sixth part;
the door should be made twenty-two units less, according to what is beautiful.
By means of the very parts of the six [elements], through the middle and the possession of the gates and so forth—how could the twenty-two gates not be made beautiful?
Furthermore, each of those— the door-panels, the cheeks, the side-wings, and so forth—
was fashioned from one-eighth parts of the most excellent glories.
For each of those, one should again fashion doors, side-walls, and so forth; the most renowned [proportion] for all of them is that they enter with an eighth part.
Even if these gateways and other features are indeed described by you according to such sequences,
they shine through the increase of what is deficient, but not through the addition of what is already excessive.
The wise have definitively taught that the doors and other features should be arranged in sequence; they should be made beautiful through proportionality—neither too small nor too large.
The fourfold division for the *abhramaṇaka* type of leg is considered to be double [that of the previous];
for that which is double, it is again six, seven, or more.
The support for that which has no surrounding ground is desired to be twice the size of the small houses; furthermore, it should be twice that again, or even six, seven, and so forth.
This quadrangular courtyard is praised when it is level with the base of the pillars;
or else, a rectangular courtyard is preferred, one side of which is considered longer.
A small house with four sides is praised; it stands upon level ground. By means of the oral instructions, even such a small house is desired as being singular once again.
That shank is indeed hollow within and moreover has a single deity as its support;
furthermore, the rotation is fourfold, and that [deity] therein is likewise one.
The very essence of that support is slightly hollow, where a single deity resides; as for the single small chamber within the courtyard, that too is likewise once again.
By the curvature of its walls, this quadrangle leads toward the courtyard; it is further enclosed on both sides by inner chambers that fill the space between the quadrangles.
In this courtyard enclosed by walls, there are small chambers accessible for passage; on both sides of the building, the interior of the small chambers is complete.
Furthermore, that which is adorned with four railings on all four sides and possesses a central recess for the pouring of water should be the support for four deities.
It is also beautifully adorned by small pavilions in the four directions; within that central core, where a single pillar is erected, are the four abodes of the gods.
In the great hall of fame (Kīrti), however, there are two pairs of four-pillared pavilions (catuṣkikā) on each side,
together with intermediate walkways, at every door in every direction.
Those renowned as very large should be provided with two small rooms each; together with their inner courtyards, they should each have doors facing their respective directions.
The beautiful *jaṅghā* (lower wall), having encircled the fourfold *samadhi*, should be made together with the wall at various intervals; this is the path of circumambulation (*bhramaṇavīthī*).

With the small central hall and the supporting pillars, it is exceedingly beautiful as it stands level with the surrounding area; the walls of the circumambulation path should be constructed together with the intermediate sections.
Thus, here, above the center of the consecration [mandala], there is a very firm fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī), whether it be a small turret or something else; everything must be exceedingly solid.
Here, upon the heart of reality, one should construct a great, stable perfume temple; whether it be a multi-storied mansion or something else, it must be made exceedingly firm.

The wall on the side of the *catuṣkī* together with the pilasters (*bhramaṇas*) should be made equal to the height of the wall, or it may be set back according to the requirements of the construction.
Lifting it together with the surrounding ground, one should build a wall on the side of the small house; the lifting walls should be made level, as one enters into the work and the site.
The *aṭu* should be constructed by a skilled artisan, according to the requirements of the work and in accordance with the height and depth of the circular walkways and the quadrangular courtyards.
The courtyards and small chambers, arranged according to their proper heights and depths, should be constructed here as is appropriate by a craftsman skilled in the knowledge of works.
For the sake of stability, and also for the work of the plinth and so forth,
an increase of one-quarter or even one-half of a part of the wall is desired for the legs [of the structure].
For the sake of stability, and also for the work of the plinth and so forth, an increase of one-quarter or even one-half of a part of the wall is desired for the legs [of the structure].
The height of the shank should be determined according to the measurement of the shank's width;
furthermore, two parts [of that] should be added above for those who are short, as agreed upon by artisans.
The height of the support is to be understood as the measure of the width of the support; furthermore, the artisans desire that two parts be made smaller above.

Above that, for the Gandhakuṭī, eight or seven parts are considered appropriate;
the *ṭhikkaryas* should be made according to those proportions, as previously stated and as will be further explained.

Above that hall of perfumed purity as well, one should desire [a structure] consisting of eight or seven parts; the manner in which the multi-storied building is constructed has also been explained as previously described.
Having thus performed this [analysis] by us through well-considered sequential stages,
the specific distinctions of the calves, the upper part, the Gandhakuṭī, and so forth, are now being described.

I have performed the sequence of the deities; according to the sequence of beautiful discernment, above the support is the clean room of the sword, which is described through the distinctions of the deities.
From the top, there are seven parts, and then again eight parts;
eighteen from the top, those [parts] across are four parts each.
Above that, the portions of seven are eightfold; furthermore, whatever [remains] constitutes eighteen above, and that too consists of fourfold portions.
Of the four outer parts, each [should be divided] into seventh and eighth [sections];
those sub-divisions of the parts are to be entered on both sides for the sake of beautiful lines. [In Tibetan:
Of the four parts on the outside, each one is the seventh and eighth; those parts should be well-circumscribed on both sides for the purpose of beautiful lines.
The four parts situated on the two sides facing forward, which are located in the middle,
are considered to be ten parts each; by these,
the shoulder is defined according to the tradition of the Vārendra artisans.
In the construction of the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) and other structures, even by later artisans,
one should indeed fashion the fragrant chamber transversely with nine parts.
Regarding the emanations such as the *gandhakuṭī*, there too the artisans shall construct a *gandhakuṭī* possessing nine parts in its width;
having introduced two parts each by means of the previously mentioned sequences,
this central mass is proclaimed by means of the five parts situated in the middle.
Following the sequence previously explained, two parts each are engaged in succession; that which abides in the center consists of five parts, and this is renowned as the aggregate (*skandha*).
Alternatively, having divided that into five parts and then removing two,
this shoulder is desired by the experts in proportions and craftsmanship to consist of three parts.
Furthermore, the parts of the five sections—there, two [sections] are for the height, and here, one-third of those three is asserted by the craftsmen as the *skandha* and the *bhuja*.
Having entered [the mandala], one should hold the thread upon the fifth [line], or else upon the third or the second;
from the two lower corners, the *gandhakuṭī* is like the tip of a lamp flame.

If, when analyzed, there is indeed no distinction among those things described as being of three kinds, then it has been shown that one should not have a differentiated cognition regarding anything that lacks differentiation; for where is there a division when there is no division? Thus it is seen that the wise do not [perceive] such [distinctions].
It is understood that [the wall] enters three parts from the top of the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*);
even with a slight entry at the base, it is not accepted as having a "barley-kernel" core (*yavagarbha*).
One should know that it enters three parts from above the fragrant chamber; even with a slight entry at the base, a "barley-kernel" [core] is not desired.
The construction of the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) may be circular or square on its sides;
this is now being analyzed for the sake of purity in accordance with the [traditional] sections.
The ritual of the circular *gandhakuṭī*, or alternatively, that which has a square ritual form, is the very purity that accords with the aggregates; now, its constituent parts shall be analyzed.
With eight parts, there are eight portions according to the prescribed rite;
it may also be made with twelve parts, exceeding [the size of] the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
Through eight parts, there are eight branches; through the actions as they are seen, there are also twelve parts, and furthermore, the perfume chamber.
It should be constructed with thirty-six [pillars] and be perfectly round and beautiful;
this Gandhakuṭī is generally seen as being square.
One should fashion a perfectly circular form consisting of thirty-six [units]; furthermore, this perfume temple should also be viewed as being square.
Or rather, one who desires such a form should construct it with that many parts;
even in the case of a temple, the construction must follow these stages and not otherwise.
One should also perform as many subsidiary parts as there are such forms desired; this sequence is that which emanates from the divine family, and not otherwise.

The increase and decrease of the middle, middle-middle, and other bands should again be made by means of quarters [of the total height] from the sides of the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) and so forth, or else for the sake of beauty.
How can one make the feet beautiful, whether they are long or short, when wearing garments such as those with stripes, or when staying in places such as the perfumed chamber?
The headband, the *icchivvara*, and so forth should be prepared according to the instruction;
other various rites should be performed as appropriate.
Woolen cloth, the central pillar, and so forth should be prepared exactly as instructed; likewise, all other various tasks should be performed precisely according to the rules.
Alternatively, in the case of those with little fame and so forth, the height of the neck may be one-quarter less.

The height of the head is desired to be exactly one full part; the height of the neck is less by one-quarter. Furthermore, for those renowned as "small" and so forth, the height of the crown of the head is held to be exactly one full part.
Having made the *skandha*, one should then divide these into five parts; three of these are for the husk (*tuṣa*).

With those [folds], one should form the neck, situated again at the end of the neck. Having formed the protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), then, from among these five parts, three [parts] should be made for the circle of the neck; it is situated at the edge near the neck.
Alternatively, this neck is desired as a grid of one unit on all sides;
it is held by the ancient artisans to be half a unit less than the shoulder portion.
The height of the neck should be one-half of the large [measurement], and not more;
the height of the head is desired to be either one-quarter less than that or half of it.

That which is the abode of immortality on the crown of the head should be like that situated within an *āmalaka* fruit; its extent is the measure of a shoulder-span, or perhaps slightly more than that.
The upper crown of the head is intended to consist of three parts of the head;
its height should be as it is beautiful,
being likewise high and low [as required].
The width of the *caitya* is one part less; the height of the *caitya* is two parts. Thus, this [measurement] applies to both length and breadth; the *caitya*, however, is [placed] above the summit.
"The width of the *caitya* is one part less; the height of the *caitya* is two parts. Here, this becomes the height and the width. It is upon the crown of the *caitya*.
One should fashion each [pillar] up to the neck;
above that, they should be stable, provided with a parasol-band, or a parasol, while the bells should be made of gold.
One should perform [the rite] for each [deity] as many times as there are necks; above that, with a firm parasol and a cloth, and upon the parasol, bells and mirrors.
Thus concludes the procedure for the characteristics of the fragrant chamber and so forth.
